variants.title: Decide or do?
variants.context: A Workflow decides; an Activity does. Workflows hold durable business state, branching, timers, retries, and compensation and must be deterministic. Activities perform external I/O and may run more than once. Use a child workflow only when the child needs its own durable lifecycle.
variants.prompt: Charging a card through the payment provider belongs where?
options: In the Workflow body.
In a child Workflow.
In an Activity.
optionFeedback: Workflow code must be deterministic and cannot call the network directly.
A child workflow is for a separate durable lifecycle, not an API call.
External I/O belongs in Activities, which tolerate timeouts and repeated attempts.
variants.hint: Is this a decision or an external operation?
variants.explanation: A Workflow decides; an Activity does.

variants.prompt: Waiting three days for approval, then branching on the answer, belongs where?
options: In an Activity that sleeps for the three days.
In a cron job that polls the approval table.
In the Workflow, using durable timers and Signals.
optionFeedback: An Activity holding a process for days is fragile and non-durable.
A polling job has nowhere to keep the branch state between runs.
Durable timers and messages are Workflow concerns and survive Worker restarts.
variants.hint: What must survive a crash during the wait?
variants.explanation: Keep durable business state and ordering in the Workflow.

Activities perform external I/O and may run more than once. Use a child workflow only when the child needs its own durable lifecycle.
variants.prompt: Each order line needs its own cancellation policy and Event History. Which construct?
options: A child Workflow per line.
A regular function inside the parent.
One Activity per line.
optionFeedback: Child Workflows earn their cost when the child needs an independent durable lifecycle.
A function shares the parent’s history and cancellation.
Activities are for I/O, not orchestration.
variants.hint: Does the child need its own lifecycle?
variants.explanation: Use a regular function for code organization; a child Workflow for an independent lifecycle.

variants.title: Reason about replay
variants.context: Replay rebuilds Workflow state from Event History. A recorded timer does not wait again; a recorded Activity result is returned from history. Direct network calls, wall-clock time, random branching, and mutable globals in Workflow code make replay non-deterministic.
variants.prompt: A Worker crashes after a 24-hour timer already fired. During replay on a new Worker, what happens to that timer?
options: The new Worker starts the 24-hour timer over again.
The Workflow fails, since the timer event is now stale.
It is read from history and does not wait again.
optionFeedback: Replay never repeats a recorded wait.
Replay is the normal recovery path, and a fired timer stays fired.
Recorded events are replayed, not re-executed.
variants.hint: What does replay use as its input?
variants.explanation: Same history, same decisions: the Workflow code re-runs against recorded Events.

variants.title: Reason about replay
variants.context: Replay rebuilds Workflow state from Event History. A recorded timer does not wait again; a recorded Activity result is returned from history. Direct network calls, wall-clock time, random branching, and mutable globals in Workflow code make replay non-deterministic.
variants.prompt: A Workflow calls Date.now() to choose a branch. Why is this dangerous?
options: Date.now() is slow enough to stall the Workflow task.
A durable timer would be cheaper than reading the clock.
Replay reads a new value and emits commands history lacks.
optionFeedback: Reading the clock is cheap; correctness under replay is the issue.
Cost is not the concern, and a timer does not decide which branch to take.
Non-deterministic branching breaks replay compatibility.
variants.hint: Would the code emit the same commands on a second run?
variants.explanation: Wall-clock APIs, randomness, network calls, and mutable globals belong outside Workflow code.

variants.title: Reason about replay
variants.context: Replay rebuilds Workflow state from Event History. A recorded timer does not wait again; a recorded Activity result is returned from history. Direct network calls, wall-clock time, random branching, and mutable globals in Workflow code make replay non-deterministic.
variants.prompt: An Activity’s result was recorded. During replay, is the Activity implementation called again?
options: No; the recorded result is returned from history.
Yes; every replay re-runs the Activity code.
Only if the original attempt was slow.
optionFeedback: Replay returns recorded results without invoking implementations.
Re-running would duplicate external effects.
How long the first attempt took has no bearing on replay.
variants.hint: What is the difference between replay and an Activity retry?
variants.explanation: Replay repeats decisions, not side effects; an Activity retry is a new attempt after an unrecorded outcome.

variants.title: Pick the timeout
variants.context: Retry Policy asks whether another attempt should run. Start-to-Close bounds one Activity attempt. Schedule-to-Close bounds the entire Activity Execution across queueing and retries. Heartbeat Timeout detects missing progress in long work.
variants.prompt: You want to detect a crashed or wedged Worker during a single Activity attempt. Which setting?
options: Retry Policy maximum attempts.
Start-to-Close timeout.
Schedule-to-Close timeout.
optionFeedback: Attempts do not detect a stuck attempt.
It bounds one attempt; set it longer than a healthy attempt.
Schedule-to-Close bounds the whole execution across attempts.
variants.hint: One attempt or the whole execution?

variants.title: Pick the timeout
variants.context: Retry Policy asks whether another attempt should run. Start-to-Close bounds one Activity attempt. Schedule-to-Close bounds the entire Activity Execution across queueing and retries. Heartbeat Timeout detects missing progress in long work.
variants.prompt: The business allows at most two hours for the entire payment step, including queueing and retries. Which setting?
options: Heartbeat timeout.
Schedule-to-Close timeout.
Start-to-Close timeout.
optionFeedback: Heartbeats detect missing progress, not the overall deadline.
It expresses the overall business time budget.
Start-to-Close bounds one attempt only.
variants.explanation: Schedule-to-Close answers “is this operation too old?”

variants.title: Pick the timeout
variants.context: Retry Policy asks whether another attempt should run. Start-to-Close bounds one Activity attempt. Schedule-to-Close bounds the entire Activity Execution across queueing and retries. Heartbeat Timeout detects missing progress in long work.
variants.prompt: A six-hour data export should fail fast if it stops making progress. Which setting?
options: Heartbeat timeout, with the Activity reporting progress.
A six-hour Start-to-Close timeout and nothing else.
No timeout, so a slow export is never cut short.
optionFeedback: Heartbeats detect stalls and can checkpoint progress for the next attempt.
A long Start-to-Close alone waits six hours to notice a stall.
Without a timeout a dead export looks identical to a slow one.
variants.hint: How would you notice a stall before the deadline?
variants.explanation: Long Activities heartbeat so stalls and cancellations are noticed promptly.

variants.title: Route the work
variants.context: A Task Queue is a routing name polled by Workers: name the capability, register implementations, measure schedule-to-start latency, then scale or isolate.
variants.prompt: GPU transcoding needs its own Workers. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Measure schedule-to-start latency, throughput, and backlog age.
Add Workers or isolate incompatible Activities based on those measurements.
Name a stable Task Queue for the capability, such as gpu-transcode.
Register the Activity implementations and credentials on Workers polling that queue.

variants.hint: The queue name is the contract between Workflow and Worker.
variants.explanation: Name → register → measure → scale or isolate. Do not use queue proliferation as a substitute for ownership.

variants.title: Route the work
variants.context: A Task Queue is a routing name polled by Workers: name the capability, register implementations, measure schedule-to-start latency, then scale or isolate.
variants.prompt: Pickup delay is growing on the payments queue. Put the response in order.

items.text: Read schedule-to-start latency and Worker saturation.
Confirm the queue name the Workflows are targeting.
Confirm Workers polling it have the payment Activities registered.
Scale Workers or reduce per-task cost.

variants.hint: Growing schedule-to-start usually means arrival exceeds capacity.

variants.title: Route the work
variants.context: A Task Queue is a routing name polled by Workers: name the capability, register implementations, measure schedule-to-start latency, then scale or isolate.
variants.prompt: A new Activity needs network access other Workers lack. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Register the Activity on Workers that have the required access.
Create a Task Queue for that capability.
Measure pickup latency on the new queue.
Scale it independently of the general pool.

variants.hint: Capability, not convenience, defines a queue.
variants.explanation: Split resource-incompatible Activities onto their own queue.

variants.title: Make effects replay-safe
variants.context: An Activity attempt can run again when its external result succeeded but Temporal did not record completion. Pass a stable operation ID downstream and make later attempts return the first result. Cancellation is cooperative; compensation is a new business action, not time travel.
variants.prompt: An Activity charged the card, but the Worker died before Temporal recorded completion. What happens next?
options: The Workflow fails permanently, since the charge is unconfirmed.
The Activity runs again, so it needs a stable operation ID.
Temporal sees the charge succeeded and moves to the next step.
optionFeedback: The retry policy runs another attempt rather than giving up.
Activities are commonly at least once across attempts.
Temporal only knows what reached its history, and completion never did.
variants.explanation: Pass a stable business operation ID downstream and store the first result.

variants.title: Make effects replay-safe
variants.context: An Activity attempt can run again when its external result succeeded but Temporal did not record completion. Pass a stable operation ID downstream and make later attempts return the first result. Cancellation is cooperative; compensation is a new business action, not time travel.
variants.prompt: A Workflow is cancelled after an Activity already committed a booking. Is the booking rolled back?
options: No; compensation is a separate business action you write.
Yes; Temporal rolls back the committed Activity work.
Yes, provided the Activity heartbeats and sees the cancel.
optionFeedback: Cancellation is cooperative and does not undo committed external work.
Temporal has no view of the booking system and undoes nothing.
Heartbeats deliver cancellation; they do not reverse effects.
variants.explanation: A request to cancel does not prove an external system rolled back work.

variants.title: Make effects replay-safe
variants.context: An Activity attempt can run again when its external result succeeded but Temporal did not record completion. Pass a stable operation ID downstream and make later attempts return the first result. Cancellation is cooperative; compensation is a new business action, not time travel.
variants.prompt: An Activity fails because the request failed validation. Should the Retry Policy keep trying?
options: Yes, with exponential backoff between attempts.
Yes, until the Schedule-to-Close budget runs out.
No; mark validation and authorization errors non-retryable.
optionFeedback: Backoff only helps transient failures.
Spending the whole budget on a deterministic failure only delays the error.
Deterministic failures do not recover with time.
variants.explanation: Configure retries from the business operation: transient errors retry, contract errors do not.
